passages.happening:
“This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass. He made it known by sending His angel to His servant John, who testifies to everything he saw. This is the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ” (verses 1-2).

“Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The first word of the book in Greek is apokalupsis, an unveiling: pulling back a cover to show what was hidden. The book is not a riddle meant to keep secrets. It is a disclosure of how things really are, and above all of who truly rules.

Notice the chain. God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ. Jesus sent it by his angel to John. John wrote it down for God's servants. And it is ‘the revelation of Jesus Christ’ in two senses: it comes from him, and it shows him.

Verse 3 gives a blessing, and it pictures how the book was first received. Most people could not read. Scripture was heard, read aloud in the church's gathering. So the blessing is on ‘the one who reads aloud’ and on ‘those who hear and obey’. The book was meant to be heard by a whole church, and kept, not only studied.

In these opening verses the book names itself in three ways at once. It is a ‘revelation’, an apocalypse, a kind of book that shows heavenly realities through visions, like Daniel. It is a ‘prophecy’, a word from God that calls for a response. And from verse 4 it is a letter, sent to seven real churches.
passages.ot:
The chain of revelation recalls the prophet Amos: “Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7).

And the book's opening echoes Daniel, the Bible's other great book of visions, where God “reveals the deep and hidden things” (Daniel 2:22) and has made known to the king “what will happen in the latter days” (Daniel 2:28).
passages.hard:
The book says these things ‘must soon come to pass’ and that ‘the time is near’. How can that be true two thousand years later?

Christians have answered in several ways, and these notes do not choose. Preterists hold that much of the book was indeed fulfilled soon, in the events around the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or the persecution and eventual fall of pagan Rome. Futurists often read ‘soon’ as meaning suddenly, or as describing the next great event in God's plan, and they point to 2 Peter 3:8, where a day with the Lord is like a thousand years. Idealists and many others read ‘near’ as describing the whole age since Christ's resurrection: the last days began with Jesus, and his return is always near, in the sense that nothing more must happen before it can come.

All agree on one thing. The first readers were meant to take the book as urgent. Its call to faithful witness and endurance, and its picture of who truly rules the world, spoke to their lives at once, not only to a distant future. Each generation since has been addressed the same way.
passages.asks: Ask whether you come to Revelation expecting a puzzle, or expecting to see Jesus Christ. Ask what it would mean to hear this book and ‘obey what is written in it’. And ask what makes it urgent for you now.

passages.t: Grace and peace from the One who is coming
passages.happening:
“John, To the seven churches in the province of Asia: Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come, and from the seven Spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (verses 4-5).

“To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood, who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father—to Him be the glory and power forever and ever! Amen” (verses 5-6).

“Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him. So shall it be! Amen. ‘I am the Alpha and the Omega,’ says the Lord God, who is and was and is to come—the Almighty” (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Now the book becomes a letter, with sender, readers and greeting. The readers are seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, the western part of what is now Turkey.

The greeting comes from three. From God, ‘who is and was and is to come’, a reworking of the name God gave Moses at the burning bush. From ‘the seven Spirits before His throne’ (see below). And from Jesus Christ. Christ is named alongside God as the source of grace.

Jesus is given three titles. ‘The faithful witness’: he told the truth about God even to death. ‘The firstborn from the dead’: the first to rise, never to die again. ‘The ruler of the kings of the earth’: in a world where the emperor claimed to rule, John says who really does. Death, resurrection and reign, in three phrases.

Then John bursts into praise. Christ ‘loves us’, now. He ‘has released us from our sins by His blood’, at the cross. And he has made his people ‘a kingdom, priests’, the very words God spoke to Israel at Sinai.

Verse 7 joins two prophets. The one ‘coming with the clouds’ is Daniel's Son of Man. ‘Those who pierced Him’ is from Zechariah. And verse 8 gives God's own title: ‘the Alpha and the Omega’, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, the beginning and the end of everything.
passages.ot:
God's name ‘who is and was and is to come’ reworks the name given to Moses: “God said to Moses, ‘I AM WHO I AM’” (Exodus 3:14).

‘A kingdom, priests’ comes from Sinai: “And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6).

The coming with the clouds is from Daniel: “I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13). And the pierced one from Zechariah: “they will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10).

‘The Alpha and the Omega’ echoes Isaiah: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 44:6).
passages.hard:
Who are ‘the seven Spirits before His throne’?

Many readers take the seven Spirits as the Holy Spirit in his fullness. Seven is the number of completeness in this book, and the picture draws on Isaiah 11:2, which names the Spirit of the LORD resting on the coming king, and on Zechariah 4, where the prophet sees a lampstand with seven lamps. On this reading the greeting comes from the Father, the Spirit and the Son together. Others take the seven Spirits as seven angelic beings who stand before God. These notes do not choose.

Either way, Christ is named alongside God as the one from whom grace and peace come. The church would later confess the Trinity in the creeds, and Revelation is one of the places that faith draws on.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that Jesus is ‘the ruler of the kings of the earth’, whoever else claims to rule. Ask whether you believe that he loves you now, and has freed you by his blood. And ask what it would mean to live as one of his ‘kingdom, priests’ this week.

passages.t: On Patmos, on the Lord's day
passages.happening:
“I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (verse 9).

“On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, saying, ‘Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea’” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
John does not write as a distant expert. He is their ‘brother and partner’. And he names three things they share: ‘the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus’. Suffering, Christ's rule, and patient endurance. Those three words sum up the book.

He was on Patmos, a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, southwest of Ephesus. He was there ‘because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus’. Most readers take that to mean he had been banished for his preaching. Roman authorities used exile to islands as a punishment for people who caused trouble. Early tradition says John was later released and went back to Ephesus.

‘The Lord’s day’ is one of the earliest uses of this name for the first day of the week, the day of Jesus' resurrection, when Christians met to worship. The Greek word for ‘the Lord's’ was used in the Roman world for things that belonged to the emperor. In a world where coins and inscriptions called the emperor lord, the phrase already quietly disputes his claim.

Then the command: write, and send it to seven churches. The cities lay roughly in a circle along a Roman road, in the order a messenger would reach them, starting at Ephesus and ending at Laodicea. A scroll carried along that road could be read aloud in each church in turn.
passages.ot:
‘In the Spirit’ is how the prophets spoke of being taken up in a vision: “Then the Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the gate of the house of the LORD that faces east” (Ezekiel 11:1).

And the voice like a trumpet recalls Sinai, when God came down to speak to his people: “there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out” (Exodus 19:16).
passages.hard:
John was suffering when he wrote. Does Revelation mean that suffering is a sign of God's anger?

No. John was on Patmos ‘because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus’. His hardship came from his faithfulness, not from God's punishment. The book calls tribulation something believers share ‘in Jesus’, alongside his kingdom and the patience to endure.

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whom you share ‘tribulation and kingdom and perseverance’ with, and whether you let them share yours. Ask what the Lord's day means to you. And ask where in your life the claim that Jesus is Lord quietly disputes someone else's claim.

passages.t: One like the Son of Man
passages.happening:
“Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man, dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest” (verses 12-13).

“The hair of His head was white like wool, as white as snow, and His eyes were like a blazing fire. His feet were like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and His voice was like the roar of many waters. He held in His right hand seven stars, and a sharp double-edged sword came from His mouth. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest” (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
John turns to see a voice, and sees a person. The picture draws heavily on the Old Testament, and the first hearers would have caught it.

‘One like the Son of Man’ is Daniel's figure, who comes to God and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus often called himself ‘the Son of Man’. But here something more is added. His hair is ‘white like wool, as white as snow’. In Daniel, that is how the Ancient of Days, God himself, is described. So the Son of Man shares God's own glory.

His long robe and golden sash suggest the dress of a priest or a king. His eyes like fire see through everything. His voice ‘like the roar of many waters’ is how Ezekiel described the sound of God's glory. The sword from his mouth is his word, which judges. And his face shines like the sun.

He stands ‘among the lampstands’. The lampstands recall the seven-branched lampstand in the tabernacle and temple. Verse 20 will say what they are: the seven churches. The risen Christ is not far off. He walks among his churches.

This is not a picture to be drawn. It is a picture to be felt: majesty, purity, power, and presence.
passages.ot:
The Son of Man and the Ancient of Days are from Daniel. “His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of His head was like pure wool” (Daniel 7:9). And “I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13).

The figure also recalls Daniel 10: “his face like the brilliance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches” (Daniel 10:6).

The voice is Ezekiel's: “His voice was like the roar of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory” (Ezekiel 43:2).

And the lampstand is from the tabernacle: “Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold” (Exodus 25:31), and Zechariah's vision of a lampstand with seven lamps (Zechariah 4:2).
passages.asks: Ask how you usually picture Jesus, and how this picture changes it. Ask what it means that he walks among the churches, including yours. And ask where his word, the sword from his mouth, needs to cut in your life.

passages.happening:
“When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man. But He placed His right hand on me and said, ‘Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades’” (verses 17-18).

“Therefore write down the things you have seen, and the things that are, and the things that will happen after this. This is the mystery of the seven stars you saw in My right hand and of the seven golden lampstands: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
John falls down ‘like a dead man’. That is how the prophets fell when they saw God's glory. And the first thing the glorified Christ does is to lay his right hand on him. The first thing he says is, ‘Do not be afraid.’

Then he says why. ‘I am the First and the Last.’ That is God's own title in Isaiah. ‘The Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever.’ He has been through death and come out the other side. ‘And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.’ Hades was the realm of the dead. Whoever holds the keys decides who goes in and who comes out. For churches facing prison and death, this was the deepest comfort the book could give.

Verse 19 tells John to write ‘the things you have seen, and the things that are, and the things that will happen after this’. Some read it as an outline of the book: chapter 1, chapters 2 and 3, and chapters 4 to 22. Others think the three phrases describe the whole book at once. Readers differ on how neatly it divides.

Then Christ explains two symbols. The lampstands are the churches. The stars in his right hand are ‘the angels of the seven churches’. The book often explains its own symbols like this, and readers should take its explanations first.
passages.ot:
‘The First and the Last’ is God's own title in Isaiah: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 44:6).

Falling down at the sight of God's glory is what Ezekiel did: “And when I saw it, I fell facedown and heard a voice speaking” (Ezekiel 1:28). And Daniel: “I fell into a deep sleep, with my face to the ground. Suddenly, a hand touched me” (Daniel 10:9-10).

God's power over death is the song of Hannah: “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6).
passages.hard:
Who are ‘the angels of the seven churches’?

The book explains that the stars are the angels, but it does not say who the angels are. The Greek word angelos means a messenger, one sent, and it is used both of heavenly beings and of human messengers. Readers have understood these angels in four main ways: as human messengers or delegates of each church; as each church's leader or bishop; as a guardian angel for each church; or as a way of speaking of each church's own spirit, the church itself. These notes do not choose.

On every reading, the point is the same. Each message is addressed to a real congregation, and Christ holds them all in his right hand.
passages.asks: Ask what you are afraid of, and hear Christ say, ‘Do not be afraid.’ Ask what it means that the one who holds the keys of death is the one who loves you. And ask whether you read hard parts of Revelation by its own explanations first.
